statement: For every natural number $k$, the set $\mathbb{N}^k$ with the [product order](c:product-order) is a [well-quasi-order](c:well-quasi-ordered-le): every infinite sequence $a_1, a_2, \dots$ in $\mathbb{N}^k$ has indices $i < j$ with $a_i \le a_j$ in every coordinate. Hence every set of [monomials](c:monomial) in $k$ variables has only finitely many minimal elements for divisibility.

hypotheses.text: The number $k$ of coordinates is finite.
Each coordinate carries the usual order of $\mathbb{N}$, which is a [well-order](c:is-well-order).

conclusion: Every infinite sequence in $\mathbb{N}^k$ has a pair $a_i \le a_j$ with $i < j$, and every set of monomials in $k$ variables has finitely many minimal elements.

formal.difference: The declaration proves that a finite product of partially well-ordered sets is partially well-ordered for the coordinatewise preorder; $\mathbb{N}^k$ is the case of $k$ copies of $\mathbb{N}$. The consequence for minimal monomials is not part of it.

proofs.name: Coordinatewise monotone subsequences
proofs.slogan: Extract a subsequence that is nondecreasing in one coordinate, refine it coordinate by coordinate, and compare two of its terms.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma, by induction on the number of coordinates. For $k = 0$ the set $\mathbb{N}^0$ is one point, so every pair is comparable.

roles.why: The well-order of $\mathbb{N}$ gives every sequence of naturals a nondecreasing subsequence.
Finitely many coordinates mean that finitely many refinements suffice.

steps.slogan: Extract a nondecreasing [subsequence](c:subsequence) from any sequence of natural numbers.
steps.detail: Let $n_1$ index a least term of the sequence $x_n$, and let $n_{m+1} > n_m$ index a least term after position $n_m$; least terms exist because $\mathbb{N}$ is well-ordered. The tail after $n_m$ lies inside the tail used to choose $n_m$, so $x_{n_m} \le x_{n_{m+1}}$.

steps.slogan: Refine the subsequence once for each of the $k$ coordinates.
steps.detail: Apply step 1 to the first coordinate of $a_n$, then to the second coordinate along the subsequence found, and so on. A subsequence of a nondecreasing sequence stays nondecreasing, so after $k$ refinements the subsequence is nondecreasing in every coordinate.

steps.slogan: Compare the first two terms of the final [monotone subsequence](c:monotone-subsequence).
steps.detail: The final subsequence $a_{m_1}, a_{m_2}, \dots$ has $m_1 < m_2$ and $a_{m_1} \le a_{m_2}$ in each coordinate, which is the inequality of the [product order](c:product-order). So no infinite sequence in $\mathbb{N}^k$ avoids such a pair.

steps.slogan: Show that the minimal [monomials](c:monomial) of a set form a finite [antichain](c:antichain).
steps.detail: The monomial $x^a$ divides $x^b$ exactly when $a \le b$ in the product order. Distinct minimal elements are incomparable, so infinitely many of them would give a sequence with no pair $a_i \le a_j$, against step 3.

concepts.c:product-order: The lemma compares exponent vectors coordinate by coordinate.
concepts.c:well-quasi-ordered-le: The conclusion is that the product order is a well-quasi-order.
concepts.c:monomial: Monomials correspond to exponent vectors, and divisibility to the product order.
concepts.c:is-well-order: The well-order of each coordinate gives least terms of tails.
concepts.c:subsequence: The proof refines the sequence by passing to subsequences.
concepts.c:monotone-subsequence: A subsequence monotone in all coordinates gives the comparable pair.
concepts.c:antichain: Minimal elements of a set are pairwise incomparable, so they form an antichain.

statement: In every finite [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) $P$, the largest size of an [antichain](c:antichain) equals the smallest number of [chains](c:chain) whose union is $P$.

hypotheses.text: The set $P$ is finite.
The relation $\le$ on $P$ is a [partial order](c:partial-order).

conclusion: The width of $P$, the largest antichain size, equals the least number of chains that cover $P$.

proofs.name: Induction on a maximal element
proofs.slogan: Remove a maximal element, cover the rest by induction, and repair the cover with the top elements of the maximum antichains.
proofs.scope: Finite posets, by strong induction on $|P|$. The empty poset has width $0$ and needs no chain.

roles.why: Finiteness gives a maximal element and makes induction on $|P|$ possible.
Transitivity and antisymmetry make $K$ a chain and make the comparisons of step 3 valid.

steps.slogan: Bound the size of any antichain by the number of chains in any cover.
steps.detail: Two elements of an [antichain](c:antichain) are incomparable, so one [chain](c:chain) holds at most one of them. Hence an antichain of size $m$ needs at least $m$ chains to be covered.

steps.slogan: Remove a maximal element $a$ and cover the rest by $w'$ chains.
steps.detail: Let $a$ be maximal in $P$ and let $Q = P \setminus \{a\}$ have width $w'$. By induction $Q$ is the union of chains $C_1, \dots, C_{w'}$, and every antichain of size $w'$ in $Q$ meets each $C_i$ exactly once.

steps.slogan: Choose in each chain the largest element that lies in a maximum antichain of $Q$.
steps.detail: Let $x_i$ be the largest element of $C_i$ in some antichain $A_i$ of size $w'$ in $Q$. If $x_i < x_j$, then $A_j$ meets $C_i$ in some $y \le x_i < x_j$, with $y$ and $x_j$ both in $A_j$, which is impossible. So $A = \{x_1, \dots, x_{w'}\}$ is an antichain.

steps.slogan: Add $a$ as a new chain when $a$ is incomparable to every $x_i$.
steps.detail: Then $A \cup \{a\}$ is an antichain of size $w' + 1$, and the chains $C_1, \dots, C_{w'}, \{a\}$ cover $P$. So $P$ has an antichain and a chain cover of the same size.

steps.slogan: Otherwise split off the chain below $a$ and cover the rest by induction.
steps.detail: As $a$ is maximal, $a > x_i$ for some $i$, and $K = \{a\} \cup \{z \in C_i : z \le x_i\}$ is a chain. Every antichain of size $w'$ in $Q$ meets $C_i$ inside $K$, so $P \setminus K$ has width below $w'$ and induction covers it by at most $w' - 1$ chains. With $K$ at most $w'$ chains cover $P$, and $A$ has size $w'$.

steps.slogan: Combine the matching antichain and cover with the lower bound of step 1.
steps.detail: In both cases $P$ has an antichain and a chain cover of the same size. By step 1 no antichain is larger than any cover, so this common size is both the width and the least number of chains.

concepts.c:partial-order: Transitivity and antisymmetry drive the comparisons between chains.
concepts.c:antichain: The largest antichain is the quantity that the chain count must match.
concepts.c:chain: The proof builds the cover from chains of the smaller poset.

source.note: The inductive proof of F. Galvin, A proof of Dilworth's chain decomposition theorem, American Mathematical Monthly 101 (1994), 352-353.

proofs.name: Bipartite matching
proofs.slogan: Encode the order as a bipartite graph, turn a maximum matching into chains, and turn a minimum vertex cover into an antichain.
proofs.scope: Finite posets; König's theorem on bipartite graphs supplies the equality of matching and cover sizes.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the bipartite graph finite, so König's theorem applies.
Transitivity and antisymmetry rule out cycles of matched pairs and make each linked sequence a chain.

steps.slogan: Build the [bipartite graph](c:bipartite-graph) with an edge $x' y''$ for each pair $x < y$.
steps.detail: Take two copies $P' = \{x'\}$ and $P'' = \{y''\}$ of $P$ and join $x'$ to $y''$ exactly when $x < y$ in $P$. Let $n = |P|$.

steps.slogan: Turn a maximum [matching](c:matching) of size $m$ into a cover by $n - m$ chains.
steps.detail: In a matching each element has at most one matched successor and one matched predecessor, so the matched pairs link $P$ into $n - m$ disjoint sequences $x_1 < x_2 < \dots$. By transitivity each sequence is a [chain](c:chain).

steps.slogan: Take a minimum [vertex cover](c:vertex-cover) of the same size $m$ by König's theorem.
steps.detail: König's theorem says that in a finite bipartite graph the largest matching and the smallest vertex cover have the same size. So some set $C$ of $m$ vertices meets every edge.

steps.slogan: Collect the elements with neither copy in the cover into an [antichain](c:antichain).
steps.detail: If $x < y$ and none of $x', x'', y', y''$ is in $C$, then the edge $x' y''$ misses $C$, which is impossible. At most $m$ elements have a copy in $C$, so at least $n - m$ pairwise incomparable elements remain.

steps.slogan: Combine the antichain and the chain cover with the counting bound.
steps.detail: Step 4 gives an antichain of size at least $n - m$, and step 2 gives a cover by $n - m$ chains. An antichain meets each chain at most once, so both numbers equal the width.

concepts.c:partial-order: The strict order relation defines the edges of the bipartite graph.
concepts.c:antichain: The vertices missed by the cover give the large antichain.
concepts.c:chain: Linked matched pairs form the chains of the cover.
concepts.c:bipartite-graph: The poset is encoded as a bipartite graph between two copies.
concepts.c:matching: A maximum matching yields the smallest chain cover.
concepts.c:vertex-cover: A minimum vertex cover yields the largest antichain.

source.note: The reduction to König's theorem of D. R. Fulkerson, Note on Dilworth's decomposition theorem for partially ordered sets, Proceedings of the AMS 7 (1956), 701-702.

statement: Let $X_t$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ solve the [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) $dX_t = b(X_t, t)\,dt + \sigma(X_t, t)\,dW_t$ and have a [density](c:probability-density-function) $p(x, t)$. Then $\partial_t p = -\sum_i \partial_i (b_i p) + \tfrac12 \sum_{i,j} \partial_i \partial_j (a_{ij} p)$ with $a = \sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}$, that is $\partial_t p = L^* p$ for the adjoint of the [generator](c:generator) $L$.

hypotheses.text: The process $X_t$ solves the [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation), with $b$ of class $C^1$ and $\sigma$ of class $C^2$ in $x$, both continuous in $t$.
The law of $X_t$ has a [density](c:probability-density-function) $p(x, t)$ that is $C^2$ in $x$ and $C^1$ in $t$.

conclusion: The density solves the forward Kolmogorov equation $\partial_t p = L^* p$.

proofs.name: Itô formula against test functions
proofs.slogan: Apply Itô's formula to a test function, take expectations, move the generator onto the density, and remove the test function.
proofs.scope: The equation holds pointwise under the stated smoothness. Without that smoothness the same steps give the equation in the weak sense of distributions.

roles.why: The SDE supplies the drift and diffusion terms of Itô's formula, and their smoothness allows the integration by parts.
The density turns expectations into integrals, and its smoothness makes $\partial_t p$ and $L^* p$ continuous.

steps.slogan: Apply Itô's formula to $\varphi(X_t)$ for a compactly supported smooth [test function](c:test-function) $\varphi$.
steps.detail: Itô's formula gives $d\varphi(X_t) = L\varphi(X_t)\,dt + \nabla\varphi(X_t)^{\mathsf T}\sigma(X_t, t)\,dW_t$, where $L\varphi = \sum_i b_i \partial_i\varphi + \tfrac12\sum_{i,j} a_{ij}\partial_i\partial_j\varphi$ is the [generator](c:generator).

steps.slogan: Take expectations and drop the [Itô integral](c:ito-integral), which has mean zero.
steps.detail: The integrand $\nabla\varphi^{\mathsf T}\sigma$ is bounded because $\varphi$ has compact support, so the Itô integral is a martingale with mean zero. Hence $\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}\,\varphi(X_t) = \mathbb{E}\,L\varphi(X_t)$.

steps.slogan: Write both expectations as integrals against the density $p$.
steps.detail: Step 2 reads $\int \varphi\,\partial_t p\,dx = \int (L\varphi)\,p\,dx$. Differentiation under the integral sign is allowed because $\varphi$ has compact support and $\partial_t p$ is continuous.

steps.slogan: Integrate by parts to move every derivative from $\varphi$ onto $b p$ and $a p$.
steps.detail: The compact support of $\varphi$ removes all boundary terms, so $\int (L\varphi)\,p\,dx = \int \varphi\,L^* p\,dx$ with $L^* p = -\sum_i \partial_i(b_i p) + \tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j(a_{ij} p)$.

steps.slogan: Remove the arbitrary test function to get $\partial_t p = L^* p$ at every point.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $\int \varphi\,(\partial_t p - L^* p)\,dx = 0$ for every test function $\varphi$. A continuous function with this property vanishes, so $\partial_t p = L^* p$.

concepts.c:stochastic-differential-equation: The SDE defines the process whose density evolves.
concepts.c:probability-density-function: The equation is a statement about the density of $X_t$.
concepts.c:generator: The density solves the equation given by the adjoint generator.
concepts.c:test-function: Test functions turn the expectation identity into a weak equation.
concepts.c:ito-integral: The martingale part of Itô's formula has mean zero and drops out.

source.note: The standard weak derivation by Itô's formula and integration by parts, as in G. A. Pavliotis, Stochastic Processes and Applications, Springer, 2014.

statement: Let $L$ be a finite [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice) and $\mu\colon L \to [0, \infty)$ a [log-supermodular](c:log-supermodular-function) weight. If $f, g\colon L \to [0, \infty)$ are [increasing](c:monotone-function), then $\big(\sum_a \mu(a) f(a)\big)\big(\sum_a \mu(a) g(a)\big) \le \big(\sum_a \mu(a)\big)\big(\sum_a \mu(a) f(a) g(a)\big)$.

hypotheses.text: The set $L$ is a finite [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice).
The weight $\mu \ge 0$ satisfies $\mu(a)\mu(b) \le \mu(a \wedge b)\,\mu(a \vee b)$ for all $a, b \in L$.
The functions $f$ and $g$ are [increasing](c:monotone-function).
The functions $f$ and $g$ take values in $[0, \infty)$.

conclusion: Under the weight $\mu$, the increasing functions $f$ and $g$ are positively correlated: the displayed inequality holds.

formal.difference: The declaration allows values in any linearly ordered commutative semiring with the same hypotheses; the statement here takes real values.

proofs.name: Four functions theorem
proofs.slogan: Check the four-function inequality for $\mu f$, $\mu g$, $\mu$ and $\mu f g$, then sum it over the lattice by the Ahlswede–Daykin theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. Nonnegativity of $f$ and $g$ can be dropped, because adding a constant to $f$ or $g$ adds the same amount to both sides.

roles.why: Distributivity is the hypothesis of the four functions theorem.
It gives the weight factor of the pointwise inequality.
It gives $f(a) \le f(a \vee b)$ and $g(b) \le g(a \vee b)$.
Nonnegative factors keep products of inequalities valid, and the four functions theorem needs nonnegative functions.

steps.slogan: Define the four functions $f_1 = \mu f$, $f_2 = \mu g$, $f_3 = \mu$ and $f_4 = \mu f g$.
steps.detail: All four functions are nonnegative because $\mu$, $f$ and $g$ are nonnegative. The claim reads $\big(\sum f_1\big)\big(\sum f_2\big) \le \big(\sum f_3\big)\big(\sum f_4\big)$.

steps.slogan: Check $f_1(a) f_2(b) \le f_3(a \wedge b)\, f_4(a \vee b)$ for all $a, b \in L$.
steps.detail: [Log-supermodularity](c:log-supermodular-function) gives $\mu(a)\mu(b) \le \mu(a \wedge b)\mu(a \vee b)$, and [monotonicity](c:monotone-function) gives $f(a) \le f(a \vee b)$ and $g(b) \le g(a \vee b)$. Multiply these inequalities between nonnegative numbers.

steps.slogan: Sum the pointwise inequality over the whole lattice with the four functions theorem.
steps.detail: The Ahlswede–Daykin theorem on a finite [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice) turns the pointwise inequality into $f_1(A) f_2(B) \le f_3(A \wedge B) f_4(A \vee B)$ for subsets $A, B$. With $A = B = L$ one has $A \wedge B = A \vee B = L$, which is the claim.

concepts.c:distributive-lattice: The four functions theorem needs a distributive lattice.
concepts.c:log-supermodular-function: Log-supermodularity of the weight gives the pointwise four-function inequality.
concepts.c:monotone-function: Monotonicity moves $f(a)$ and $g(b)$ up to the join.

source.note: mathlib applies four_functions_theorem_univ to $\mu f$, $\mu g$, $\mu$ and $\mu f g$ and checks the pointwise inequality with mul_le_mul.

statement: The functor $X \mapsto C(X)$ is a [duality](c:duality-of-categories) (a contravariant equivalence) between [compact Hausdorff spaces](c:compact-hausdorff-space) with continuous maps and [commutative](c:comm-c-star-algebra) unital C*-algebras with unital *-homomorphisms. Its inverse sends $A$ to its [Gelfand spectrum](c:gelfand-spectrum) $\Omega(A)$, the set of characters of $A$ with the [weak-star topology](c:weak-star-topology).

hypotheses.text: The spaces are [compact Hausdorff spaces](c:compact-hausdorff-space), and the maps between them are continuous.
The algebras are [commutative](c:comm-c-star-algebra) unital C*-algebras, and the morphisms are unital *-homomorphisms.

conclusion: Naturally in $A$ and $X$, one has $A \cong C(\Omega(A))$ and $X \cong \Omega(C(X))$, so the two categories are dual.

proofs.name: Gelfand transform and evaluation
proofs.slogan: Show that the Gelfand transform $A \to C(\Omega(A))$ and the evaluation map $X \to \Omega(C(X))$ are natural isomorphisms.
proofs.scope: The whole duality, with complex scalars. The empty space corresponds to the zero algebra, which has no characters.

roles.why: Compactness gives the common-zero argument and the homeomorphism criterion; the Hausdorff property gives Urysohn's lemma.
Commutativity lets characters detect the algebra, and the C*-identity makes the Gelfand transform isometric.

steps.slogan: Show that the character space $\Omega(A)$ is a compact Hausdorff space.
steps.detail: A character is a nonzero multiplicative linear functional of norm $1$; its kernel is a [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal), and by Gelfand–Mazur every maximal ideal arises so. The characters form a weak-star closed subset of the unit ball of $A^*$, which is compact by Banach–Alaoglu and Hausdorff.

steps.slogan: Prove that the Gelfand transform $a \mapsto \hat a$ is an isometric *-isomorphism onto $C(\Omega(A))$.
steps.detail: Here $\hat a(\chi) = \chi(a)$, and characters are real on self-adjoint elements, so the map keeps the star. Gelfand's formula and the C*-identity give $\|\hat a\|_\infty = r(a) = \|a\|$ for self-adjoint $a$, hence for all $a$ through $a^*a$. The closed image separates points and contains constants, so it is everything by Stone–Weierstrass.

steps.slogan: Prove that evaluation $x \mapsto \mathrm{ev}_x$ is a homeomorphism from $X$ onto $\Omega(C(X))$.
steps.detail: Urysohn's lemma makes the map injective, and it is weak-star continuous. A maximal ideal without common zero would contain, by compactness, finitely many $f_i$ with $\sum |f_i|^2$ invertible, so every character is an evaluation; a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism.

steps.slogan: Define both functors on morphisms by composition with $h$ and with $\phi$.
steps.detail: Composition $f \mapsto f \circ h$ with $h\colon X \to Y$ is a unital *-homomorphism $C(Y) \to C(X)$. Composition $\chi \mapsto \chi \circ \phi$ with $\phi\colon A \to B$ maps characters of $B$ to characters of $A$ and is weak-star continuous, so both constructions are contravariant functors.

steps.slogan: Check that both isomorphisms commute with the induced maps, which gives the duality.
steps.detail: For $\phi\colon A \to B$ one has $\widehat{\phi(a)}(\chi) = \hat a(\chi \circ \phi)$, and for $h\colon X \to Y$ one has $\mathrm{ev}_{h(x)} = \mathrm{ev}_x \circ h^*$. So the Gelfand transform and evaluation are natural isomorphisms, and the two functors are inverse [dualities](c:duality-of-categories).

concepts.c:duality-of-categories: The result is a contravariant equivalence of the two categories.
concepts.c:compact-hausdorff-space: Compact Hausdorff spaces are exactly the spaces recovered from their function algebras.
concepts.c:comm-c-star-algebra: Commutative unital C*-algebras are exactly the algebras of the form $C(X)$.
concepts.c:gelfand-spectrum: The spectrum is the space that the inverse functor assigns to an algebra.
concepts.c:weak-star-topology: The weak-star topology makes the spectrum compact and the transforms continuous.
concepts.c:maximal-ideal: Characters correspond to maximal ideals through their kernels.

source.note: The standard proof through the commutative Gelfand–Naimark theorem, as in G. J. Murphy, C*-Algebras and Operator Theory, Academic Press, 1990, chapters 1 and 2.

statement: Every [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) $A$ is isometrically *-isomorphic to a norm-closed *-subalgebra of the algebra $B(H)$ of [bounded operators](c:bounded-operator) on some [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$.

hypotheses.text: The algebra $A$ is a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra): a Banach *-algebra with $\|a^* a\| = \|a\|^2$ for every $a$.

conclusion: Some injective *-homomorphism $\pi\colon A \to B(H)$ has $\|\pi(a)\| = \|a\|$, so $\pi(A)$ is a closed *-subalgebra isomorphic to $A$.

proofs.name: Universal GNS representation
proofs.slogan: Build the GNS representation of every state, take their direct sum, and use states that see the norm to make the sum isometric.
proofs.scope: Unital $A$. A nonunital algebra sits isometrically in its [unitization](c:unitization-of-a-c-star-algebra), and the restriction of the result proves the claim.

roles.why: The C*-identity gives $\|a^*a\| = \|a\|^2$, bounds the GNS operators and lets states see the norm.

steps.slogan: Find for each $a \in A$ a [state](c:state-on-a-star-algebra) $\varphi$ with $\varphi(a^* a) = \|a\|^2$.
steps.detail: By Gelfand duality the C*-algebra generated by $1$ and $a^*a$ is $C(\sigma(a^*a))$, and $\|a^*a\| \in \sigma(a^*a)$, so evaluation there is a character with value $\|a\|^2$. Extend it by Hahn–Banach to a functional of norm $1$ with $\varphi(1) = 1$, which is positive.

steps.slogan: Build the [GNS](c:gns-construction) representation $\pi_\varphi$ on a Hilbert space $H_\varphi$ for each state.
steps.detail: The form $\langle b, c\rangle = \varphi(c^* b)$ is positive semidefinite; divide by its null space and complete to get $H_\varphi$. Left multiplication $\pi_\varphi(a)[b] = [ab]$ has $\|\pi_\varphi(a)\| \le \|a\|$ and gives a *-representation with $\langle \pi_\varphi(a)\xi, \xi\rangle = \varphi(a)$ for $\xi = [1]$.

steps.slogan: Take the [direct sum](c:direct-sum) $\pi = \bigoplus_\varphi \pi_\varphi$ over all states.
steps.detail: On $H = \bigoplus_\varphi H_\varphi$ the operators $\pi(a)$ act coordinatewise and satisfy $\|\pi(a)\| \le \|a\|$. So $\pi\colon A \to B(H)$ is a *-homomorphism.

steps.slogan: Show that $\pi$ is isometric, so its image is a closed *-subalgebra isomorphic to $A$.
steps.detail: For the state $\varphi$ of step 1, the unit vector $\xi_\varphi$ has $\|\pi(a)\xi_\varphi\|^2 = \varphi(a^*a) = \|a\|^2$, so $\|\pi(a)\| \ge \|a\|$. An isometry is injective, and its image is complete, hence closed.

concepts.c:c-star-algebra: The C*-identity is what makes the representation isometric.
concepts.c:bounded-operator: The algebra is realized by bounded operators on the sum space.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: Each state gives a Hilbert space, and the theorem uses their sum.
concepts.c:unitization-of-a-c-star-algebra: The unitization reduces the nonunital case to the unital case.
concepts.c:state-on-a-star-algebra: States that attain $\|a\|^2$ at $a^*a$ detect the norm.
concepts.c:gns-construction: The GNS construction turns each state into a representation.
concepts.c:direct-sum: The direct sum combines all GNS representations into one faithful one.

source.note: The Gelfand–Naimark–Segal proof, as in G. J. Murphy, C*-Algebras and Operator Theory, Academic Press, 1990, section 3.4.

statement: Let $D \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded region whose boundary $C$ is a positively oriented, piecewise smooth [simple closed curve](c:simple-closed-curve), and let $P$ and $Q$ have continuous [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative) on an open set that contains $D$. Then $\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D \big(\partial_x Q - \partial_y P\big)\,dA$.

hypotheses.text: The region $D$ is bounded by a positively oriented, piecewise smooth [simple closed curve](c:simple-closed-curve) $C$.
The functions $P$ and $Q$ have continuous [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative) on an open set that contains $D$.

conclusion: The [line integral](c:line-integral) of $P\,dx + Q\,dy$ around $C$ equals the [double integral](c:double-integral) of $\partial_x Q - \partial_y P$ over $D$.

proofs.name: Elementary regions
proofs.slogan: Integrate $\partial_y P$ along vertical lines and $\partial_x Q$ along horizontal lines, then glue elementary regions along cuts that cancel.
proofs.scope: Regions that split into finitely many regions, each of type I and of type II, which covers the regions met in calculus. A general Jordan region needs an extra approximation by such regions, which this proof does not write out.

roles.why: The positive orientation fixes the signs of the boundary pieces, and the region splits into elementary regions.
Continuous partial derivatives make $\partial_y P$ and $\partial_x Q$ integrable and allow the fundamental theorem of calculus.

steps.slogan: Integrate $\partial_y P$ along vertical lines over a type I region.
steps.detail: Let $D = \{a \le x \le b,\ g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)\}$. Fubini's theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus give $\iint_D \partial_y P\,dA = \int_a^b \big(P(x, g_2(x)) - P(x, g_1(x))\big)\,dx$.

steps.slogan: Compute $\oint_C P\,dx$ on the four boundary pieces of the type I region.
steps.detail: The lower graph gives $\int_a^b P(x, g_1(x))\,dx$, the upper graph, run backwards, gives $-\int_a^b P(x, g_2(x))\,dx$, and the vertical sides give $0$ because $dx = 0$ there. So $\oint_C P\,dx = -\iint_D \partial_y P\,dA$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the argument along horizontal lines to get $\oint_C Q\,dy = \iint_D \partial_x Q\,dA$.
steps.detail: For a type II region $\{c \le y \le d,\ h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)\}$ the same computation with $x$ and $y$ exchanged gives this identity. The positive orientation now runs the right graph upwards, so the sign is $+$.

steps.slogan: Add the two identities on a region of both types.
steps.detail: A region of type I and type II satisfies both identities. Their sum is Green's formula $\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D (\partial_x Q - \partial_y P)\,dA$ for that region.

steps.slogan: Cut $D$ into elementary regions and add their formulas so that the interior cuts cancel.
steps.detail: The [double integrals](c:double-integral) over the pieces add up to the integral over $D$. Each interior cut is run twice in opposite directions, so its [line integrals](c:line-integral) cancel and the boundary terms add up to $\oint_C$.

concepts.c:simple-closed-curve: The boundary curve and its orientation fix the signs of the pieces.
concepts.c:partial-derivative: The integrand $\partial_x Q - \partial_y P$ is made of partial derivatives.
concepts.c:line-integral: The left side is the line integral around the boundary.
concepts.c:double-integral: The right side is the double integral computed by iterated integration.

source.note: The standard proof for elementary regions, as in T. M. Apostol, Calculus, Volume II, 2nd edition, Wiley, 1969, chapter 11.

statement: Let a [group](c:group) $G$ [act](c:group-action) on a set $X$ and let $x \in X$. Then $g G_x \mapsto g \cdot x$ is a well-defined bijection from the left [cosets](c:coset) of the [stabilizer](c:stabilizer) $G_x$ onto the [orbit](c:orbit) $G \cdot x$. Hence $|G \cdot x| = [G : G_x]$, and $|G| = |G \cdot x|\,|G_x|$ when $G$ is finite.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ [acts](c:group-action) on $X$: $e \cdot y = y$ and $g \cdot (h \cdot y) = (gh) \cdot y$ for all $g, h, y$.
For the product formula, the group $G$ is finite.

conclusion: The orbit of $x$ is in bijection with $G/G_x$, so its size is the [index](c:index-of-a-subgroup) of the stabilizer.

formal.difference: The declaration gives the bijection only. The product formula $|G \cdot x|\,|G_x| = |G|$ is the separate declaration MulAction.card_orbit_mul_card_stabilizer_eq_card_group.

proofs.name: Coset map
proofs.slogan: Send each coset $g G_x$ to $g \cdot x$, and show that this map is well defined, injective and onto the orbit.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The equality $|G \cdot x| = [G : G_x]$ holds for infinite $G$ as an equality of cardinals, and only the product formula needs $G$ finite.

roles.why: The action axioms make $G_x$ a subgroup and let $h^{-1}$ cancel in $g \cdot x = h \cdot x$.
Finiteness turns the index into the quotient $|G|/|G_x|$.

steps.slogan: Show that the stabilizer $G_x = \{g : g \cdot x = x\}$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup).
steps.detail: The action axioms give $e \cdot x = x$, $(gh) \cdot x = g \cdot (h \cdot x) = x$ for $g, h \in G_x$, and $g^{-1} \cdot x = g^{-1} \cdot (g \cdot x) = x$. So the cosets $g G_x$ are defined.

steps.slogan: Prove that $g \cdot x = h \cdot x$ holds exactly when $g G_x = h G_x$.
steps.detail: Acting by $h^{-1}$ shows that $g \cdot x = h \cdot x$ is equivalent to $(h^{-1} g) \cdot x = x$, that is $h^{-1} g \in G_x$. This is the condition $g G_x = h G_x$, so the map is well defined and injective.

steps.slogan: Show that every point $g \cdot x$ of the orbit is the image of the coset $g G_x$.
steps.detail: The orbit is $G \cdot x = \{g \cdot x : g \in G\}$ by definition, and $g G_x$ maps to $g \cdot x$. So the map is onto the orbit.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the orbit and the set of cosets have the same size.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 make $g G_x \mapsto g \cdot x$ a bijection $G/G_x \to G \cdot x$. So $|G \cdot x|$ is the number of left cosets, the [index](c:index-of-a-subgroup) $[G : G_x]$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the index by $|G_x|$ with Lagrange's theorem when $G$ is finite.
steps.detail: The left cosets of $G_x$ partition $G$ into blocks of size $|G_x|$, so $|G| = [G : G_x]\,|G_x| = |G \cdot x|\,|G_x|$.

concepts.c:group: The group structure gives inverses that cancel in the action.
concepts.c:group-action: The action axioms are the only facts about $X$ that the proof uses.
concepts.c:coset: Cosets of the stabilizer label the points of the orbit.
concepts.c:stabilizer: The stabilizer measures which group elements give the same point.
concepts.c:orbit: The orbit is the set that the coset map hits.
concepts.c:index-of-a-subgroup: The orbit size equals the index of the stabilizer.
concepts.c:subgroup: The stabilizer must be a subgroup for its cosets to exist.

source.note: mathlib builds the map ofQuotientStabilizer from $G/G_x$ to the orbit, proves it injective (injective_ofQuotientStabilizer) and onto, and applies Equiv.ofBijective.

statement: Let $T$ be a [first-order theory](c:first-order-theory) and $\varphi$ a sentence of its language. If every [model](c:model) of $T$ satisfies $\varphi$, then $\varphi$ has a [formal proof](c:formal-proof) from the axioms of $T$.

hypotheses.text: The theory $T$ is a set of first-order sentences, and $\varphi$ is a sentence of the same language.
Every [model](c:model) of $T$ satisfies $\varphi$.

conclusion: The sentence $\varphi$ is provable from $T$, that is $T \vdash \varphi$.

proofs.name: Henkin construction
proofs.slogan: Assume that $\varphi$ is unprovable, extend $T \cup \{\neg\varphi\}$ to a maximal consistent theory with witnesses, and build a model from its terms.
proofs.scope: Languages of any size, with Zorn's lemma for the maximal extension. For a countable language an enumeration of the sentences replaces Zorn's lemma.

roles.why: First-order syntax gives finite proofs, the deduction theorem and the closed terms of the model.
The term model is a model of $T$, so it would have to satisfy $\varphi$.

steps.slogan: Assume $T \nvdash \varphi$ and show that $T \cup \{\neg\varphi\}$ is a [consistent theory](c:consistent-theory).
steps.detail: If $T \cup \{\neg\varphi\}$ proved a contradiction, the deduction theorem would give $T \vdash \neg\varphi \to \bot$, hence $T \vdash \varphi$. This contradicts the assumption.

steps.slogan: Add a new constant $c_\psi$ and the axiom $\exists x\,\psi \to \psi(c_\psi)$ for every formula $\psi$.
steps.detail: If an added axiom gave a contradiction, then $T \vdash \exists x\,\psi$ and $T \vdash \neg\psi(c_\psi)$, and since $c_\psi$ is new, generalization gives $T \vdash \forall x\,\neg\psi$, which is absurd. Repeating this [Henkin construction](c:henkin-construction) countably often gives a consistent theory with a witness for every existential sentence.

steps.slogan: Extend the witnessed theory to a [maximal consistent set](c:maximal-consistent-formulae) $T^*$ by Zorn's lemma.
steps.detail: Consistent extensions, ordered by inclusion, have unions as upper bounds, because a proof uses finitely many axioms. A maximal element $T^*$ contains $\psi$ or $\neg\psi$ for every sentence $\psi$ and keeps the witnesses.

steps.slogan: Build the [term model](c:term-model) on closed terms modulo provable equality in $T^*$.
steps.detail: Let the domain be the closed terms modulo $s \sim t$ when $s = t \in T^*$, and interpret function and relation symbols as $T^*$ prescribes. The equality axioms make these interpretations well defined.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction on formulas that the term model satisfies exactly the sentences of $T^*$.
steps.detail: Atomic sentences hold by construction, negation and conjunction follow from maximality and consistency, and $\exists x\,\psi$ follows from the witness $c_\psi$. So the term model is a model of $T \cup \{\neg\varphi\}$.

steps.slogan: Contradict the hypothesis that every model of $T$ satisfies $\varphi$.
steps.detail: The term model satisfies $T$ but not $\varphi$, which the hypothesis excludes. So the assumption $T \nvdash \varphi$ fails, and $T \vdash \varphi$.

concepts.c:first-order-theory: The theorem concerns provability from a set of first-order axioms.
concepts.c:model: Validity in every model is the hypothesis the term model contradicts.
concepts.c:formal-proof: The conclusion is the existence of a formal proof.
concepts.c:consistent-theory: An unprovable sentence makes its negation consistent with $T$.
concepts.c:henkin-construction: Henkin witnesses make existential sentences true in the term model.
concepts.c:maximal-consistent-formulae: A maximal consistent set decides every sentence, as a truth assignment must.
concepts.c:term-model: The model is built from the closed terms of the language.

source.note: Henkin's proof (L. Henkin, The completeness of the first-order functional calculus, Journal of Symbolic Logic 14 (1949), 159-166), as in H. B. Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic, chapter 2.

statement: If $n$ is even, every continuous tangent [vector field](c:vector-field) on the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ vanishes somewhere: no continuous $v\colon S^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ has $v(x) \perp x$ and $v(x) \ne 0$ for every $x \in S^n$.

hypotheses.text: The dimension $n$ is even.
The field $v\colon S^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is continuous.
The field is tangent to the [sphere](c:sphere): $v(x) \perp x$ for every $x \in S^n$.

proofs.name: Degree of the antipodal map
proofs.slogan: Rotate each point toward its unit tangent vector to deform the identity into the antipodal map, and compare the two degrees.
proofs.scope: Even $n \ge 2$, by degree theory. For $n = 0$ the condition $v(x) \perp x$ in $\mathbb{R}$ already forces $v = 0$.

roles.why: Even $n$ makes $(-1)^{n+1} = -1$, which differs from $\deg(\mathrm{id}) = 1$.
Continuity of $v$ makes the unit field $u$ and the deformation $F$ continuous.
Orthogonality of $x$ and $u(x)$ keeps $F(x, t)$ on the unit sphere.

steps.slogan: Assume that $v$ has no zero and replace it by the unit field $u = v/|v|$.
steps.detail: Division by the continuous nonzero function $|v|$ keeps continuity. The new field satisfies $u(x) \perp x$ and $|u(x)| = 1$ for every $x$.

steps.slogan: Deform the identity into the [antipodal map](c:antipodal-map) by $F(x, t) = \cos(\pi t)\,x + \sin(\pi t)\,u(x)$.
steps.detail: Since $x \perp u(x)$ and both are unit vectors, $|F(x, t)|^2 = \cos^2(\pi t) + \sin^2(\pi t) = 1$, so $F$ maps into $S^n$. It is continuous with $F(\cdot, 0) = \mathrm{id}$ and $F(\cdot, 1) = -\mathrm{id}$, so it is a [homotopy](c:homotopy).

steps.slogan: Compute the [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) of the antipodal map as $(-1)^{n+1}$.
steps.detail: The antipodal map is the composite of the $n + 1$ reflections $x_i \mapsto -x_i$. Each reflection has degree $-1$ and degree is multiplicative, so $\deg(-\mathrm{id}) = (-1)^{n+1} = -1$ for even $n$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two degrees through the [homotopy invariance](c:homotopy-invariance) of homology.
steps.detail: Homotopic maps induce the same map on $H_n(S^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}$, so they have the same degree. But $\deg(\mathrm{id}) = 1 \ne -1$, so $v$ must have a zero.

concepts.c:vector-field: The theorem forbids a nowhere-zero continuous tangent vector field.
concepts.c:sphere: The sphere is the space whose tangent fields the proof studies.
concepts.c:antipodal-map: The tangent field deforms the identity into the antipodal map.
concepts.c:homotopy: The rotation toward $u(x)$ is a homotopy from the identity.
concepts.c:degree-of-a-map: Degree is the integer invariant that separates the two maps.
concepts.c:homotopy-invariance: Homotopic maps must have equal degree, which gives the contradiction.

source.note: The degree proof in A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Cambridge University Press, 2002, theorem 2.28.

statement: For locally integrable $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ let $Mf(x) = \sup_{r > 0} |B(x, r)|^{-1} \int_{B(x, r)} |f|$. If $f \in L^1$, then $Mf$ satisfies the [weak-type estimate](c:weak-type-estimate) $|\{Mf > \lambda\}| \le 3^n \|f\|_1/\lambda$ for every $\lambda > 0$. If $f$ lies in the [Lp space](c:lp-space) $L^p$ with $1 < p \le \infty$, then $\|Mf\|_p \le C_{n,p} \|f\|_p$.

hypotheses.text: For the weak-type bound, $f \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$.
For the strong bound, $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ with $1 < p \le \infty$.

conclusion: The maximal operator is of weak type $(1, 1)$ with constant $3^n$ and bounded on $L^p$ for $1 < p \le \infty$.

proofs.name: Vitali covering and a level split
proofs.slogan: Cover a compact part of each level set by balls with large averages, keep disjoint ones by Vitali, then split $f$ at each level for $L^p$.
proofs.scope: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$. The proof gives $C_{n,p}^p = 2^p 3^n p/(p - 1)$ for $p < \infty$ and $C_{n,\infty} = 1$.

roles.why: Integrability makes $\|f\|_1$ finite in the weak-type bound.
For $f \in L^p$ the large part $f_1$ is integrable and $\|f\|_p^p$ is the final integral; for $p = \infty$ the bound is direct.

steps.slogan: Show that each level set $\{Mf > \lambda\}$ is open.
steps.detail: If the average of $|f|$ over $B(x, r)$ exceeds $\lambda$, then for $x'$ near $x$ a slightly larger ball around $x'$ contains $B(x, r)$ and still has average above $\lambda$. So $Mf$ is [lower semicontinuous](c:lower-semicontinuous-function) and measurable.

steps.slogan: Select disjoint balls whose triples cover a compact subset $K$ of the level set.
steps.detail: Each $x \in K$ is the center of a ball $B$ with $\int_B |f| > \lambda |B|$. Finitely many of these balls cover $K$, and the Vitali covering lemma selects disjoint ones $B_1, \dots, B_m$ with $K \subseteq \bigcup_i 3B_i$.

steps.slogan: Sum the measures of the tripled balls to bound $|K|$ by $3^n \|f\|_1/\lambda$.
steps.detail: Since the $B_i$ are disjoint, $|K| \le 3^n \sum_i |B_i| < 3^n \lambda^{-1} \sum_i \int_{B_i} |f| \le 3^n \|f\|_1/\lambda$. [Inner regularity](c:inner-regularity) of [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) extends the bound to the open level set.

steps.slogan: Bound $Mf$ by $\|f\|_\infty$ directly.
steps.detail: Every average of $|f|$ over a ball is at most $\|f\|_\infty$, so $\|Mf\|_\infty \le \|f\|_\infty$. This is the case $p = \infty$ with constant $1$.

steps.slogan: Split $f$ at height $\lambda/2$ and apply the weak bound to the large part.
steps.detail: Write $f = f_1 + f_2$ with $f_1 = f\,\mathbf{1}_{\{|f| > \lambda/2\}}$, which is integrable when $f \in L^p$. Step 4 gives $Mf_2 \le \lambda/2$, so $\{Mf > \lambda\} \subseteq \{Mf_1 > \lambda/2\}$, and step 3 bounds its measure by $2 \cdot 3^n \lambda^{-1} \int_{\{|f| > \lambda/2\}} |f|$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the level estimate against $p \lambda^{p-1}\,d\lambda$ and exchange the integrals.
steps.detail: By the layer-cake formula and Tonelli's theorem, $\|Mf\|_p^p = p \int_0^\infty \lambda^{p-1} |\{Mf > \lambda\}|\,d\lambda \le 2 \cdot 3^n p \int |f| \int_0^{2|f|} \lambda^{p-2}\,d\lambda\,dx$. The inner integral is $(2|f|)^{p-1}/(p - 1)$, so $\|Mf\|_p^p \le 2^p 3^n \tfrac{p}{p-1} \|f\|_p^p$.

concepts.c:weak-type-estimate: The first conclusion is a weak-type bound on level sets.
concepts.c:lp-space: The second conclusion bounds $Mf$ in the $L^p$ norm.
concepts.c:lower-semicontinuous-function: Lower semicontinuity makes the level sets open and measurable.
concepts.c:inner-regularity: Inner regularity reduces the open level set to compact subsets.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Balls scale by $3^n$ in Lebesgue measure when tripled.

source.note: The standard proof, as in E. M. Stein, Singular Integrals and Differentiability Properties of Functions, Princeton University Press, 1970, chapter I.

statement: Let $E$ be an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) over the [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{F}_q$, and let $N = \#E(\mathbb{F}_q)$ be the number of its points over $\mathbb{F}_q$, including the point at infinity. Then $|N - (q + 1)| \le 2\sqrt{q}$.

hypotheses.text: The base field $\mathbb{F}_q$ is a [finite field](c:finite-field) with $q$ elements.
The curve $E$ is an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) defined over $\mathbb{F}_q$.

proofs.name: Frobenius and the degree form
proofs.slogan: Count the points as the degree of $1 - \phi$ for the Frobenius $\phi$, and bound that degree by Cauchy–Schwarz for the degree quadratic form.
proofs.scope: All elliptic curves over finite fields. The proof uses the standard theory of isogenies and dual isogenies.

roles.why: The finite field supplies the Frobenius map, whose fixed points are the rational points.
The group law and the isogeny theory of $E$ give separability, dual isogenies and the degree form.

steps.slogan: Express $E(\mathbb{F}_q)$ as the kernel of $1 - \phi$ for the [Frobenius endomorphism](c:frobenius) $\phi$.
steps.detail: The map $\phi(x, y) = (x^q, y^q)$ is an endomorphism of $E$ of degree $q$ because $E$ is defined over $\mathbb{F}_q$. A point of $E(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q)$ is fixed by $\phi$ exactly when its coordinates lie in $\mathbb{F}_q$, so $E(\mathbb{F}_q) = \ker(1 - \phi)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $1 - \phi$ is separable, so that $N = \deg(1 - \phi)$.
steps.detail: The invariant differential satisfies $\phi^*\omega = 0$, so $(1 - \phi)^*\omega = \omega \ne 0$ and the [isogeny](c:isogeny) $1 - \phi$ is separable. A separable isogeny has as many kernel points as its degree, so $N = \deg(1 - \phi)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the degree is a positive definite [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) on $\mathrm{End}(E)$.
steps.detail: With dual isogenies, $\deg\psi = \hat\psi\psi$, and $(\psi, \chi) \mapsto \deg(\psi + \chi) - \deg\psi - \deg\chi = \hat\psi\chi + \hat\chi\psi$ is bilinear. Also $\deg\psi \ge 0$, with equality only for $\psi = 0$.

steps.slogan: Apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the degree form with $\psi = 1$ and $\chi = -\phi$.
steps.detail: For a positive semidefinite quadratic form, $|\deg(\psi + \chi) - \deg\psi - \deg\chi| \le 2\sqrt{\deg\psi\,\deg\chi}$. With $\deg 1 = 1$, $\deg(-\phi) = q$ and $\deg(1 - \phi) = N$, this reads $|N - q - 1| \le 2\sqrt{q}$.

concepts.c:elliptic-curve: The rational points of the elliptic curve are the objects counted.
concepts.c:finite-field: The finite base field gives the Frobenius endomorphism.
concepts.c:frobenius: Rational points are the fixed points of Frobenius.
concepts.c:isogeny: Separable isogenies have kernels of size equal to their degree.
concepts.c:quadratic-form: Positivity of the degree form gives the Cauchy–Schwarz bound.

source.note: Hasse's bound through the Frobenius endomorphism, as in J. H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, Springer, 1986, theorem V.1.1.

statement: Let $f\colon M \to N$ be a [continuous](c:continuous-function) map between [metric spaces](c:metric-space), with $M$ [compact](c:compact-space). Then $f$ is [uniformly continuous](c:uniform-continuity): for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $d(f(x), f(y)) < \varepsilon$ whenever $d(x, y) < \delta$.

hypotheses.text: The domain $M$ is a [compact](c:compact-space) metric space.
The map $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).

formal.difference: The declaration is stated for a compact uniform space and any uniform codomain, which include metric spaces, so it proves more than this statement.

proofs.name: Neighborhoods of the diagonal
proofs.slogan: Pull back the $\varepsilon$-neighborhood of the diagonal of $N$ by $f \times f$, and show that it contains a $\delta$-neighborhood of the diagonal of $M$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $M$ is empty, every $\delta$ works.

roles.why: Compactness of $M \times M$ makes the complement of $U$ compact, so the distance has a positive minimum there.
Continuity makes $f \times f$ continuous, so the pullback $U$ is open.

steps.slogan: Show that $f \times f$ is continuous and maps the diagonal of $M$ into the diagonal of $N$.
steps.detail: The map $(x, y) \mapsto (f(x), f(y))$ is continuous on $M \times M$ because both components are [continuous](c:continuous-function). It sends each pair $(x, x)$ to $(f(x), f(x))$.

steps.slogan: Pull back the open set $V = \{(u, v) : d(u, v) < \varepsilon\}$ to an open neighborhood $U$ of the diagonal.
steps.detail: The set $V$ is open and contains the diagonal of $N$. By step 1, $U = (f \times f)^{-1}(V)$ is open in $M \times M$ and contains the diagonal of $M$.

steps.slogan: Find $\delta > 0$ with $\{d < \delta\} \subseteq U$ by minimizing $d$ on the complement of $U$.
steps.detail: The complement $F = (M \times M) \setminus U$ is closed in the [compact](c:compact-space) space $M \times M$, so it is compact, and $d > 0$ on $F$ because $F$ misses the diagonal. If $F$ is nonempty, $d$ attains a positive minimum $\delta$ on $F$; otherwise any $\delta$ works.

steps.slogan: Read off uniform continuity from the inclusion $\{d < \delta\} \subseteq U$.
steps.detail: If $d(x, y) < \delta$, then $(x, y) \in U$, so $d(f(x), f(y)) < \varepsilon$. The number $\delta$ depends on $\varepsilon$ only, not on $x$ or $y$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $f$ is the local property that compactness makes uniform.
concepts.c:metric-space: Distances on both sides give the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form of uniform continuity.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of the domain turns pointwise continuity into uniform continuity.
concepts.c:uniform-continuity: Uniform continuity is the conclusion: one $\delta$ for each $\varepsilon$.

source.note: mathlib rewrites the uniformity of the compact space as the neighborhood filter of the diagonal (nhdsSet_diagonal_eq_uniformity), pushes it forward by the continuous map Prod.map f f, and ends with nhdsSet_diagonal_le_uniformity.

proofs.name: Convergent subsequences
proofs.slogan: Assume that uniform continuity fails, take pairs of points that approach each other while their images stay apart, and pass to a convergent subsequence.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by contradiction. It uses that a compact metric space is sequentially compact.

roles.why: Compactness gives a convergent subsequence of the points $x_k$.
Continuity at the limit point sends both image sequences to $f(x)$.

steps.slogan: Negate uniform continuity to get pairs $x_k, y_k$ with $d(x_k, y_k) < 1/k$ and distant images.
steps.detail: If $f$ is not uniformly continuous, some $\varepsilon > 0$ fails for every $\delta = 1/k$. So for each $k$ there are points with $d(x_k, y_k) < 1/k$ and $d(f(x_k), f(y_k)) \ge \varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Extract a [subsequence](c:subsequence) $x_{k_j}$ that converges to a point $x \in M$.
steps.detail: A compact metric space is [sequentially compact](c:seq-compact-space), so $x_{k_j} \to x$ for some subsequence. Since $d(y_{k_j}, x_{k_j}) < 1/k_j$, also $y_{k_j} \to x$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit in $d(f(x_{k_j}), f(y_{k_j})) \ge \varepsilon$ by continuity at $x$.
steps.detail: [Continuity](c:continuous-function) gives $f(x_{k_j}) \to f(x)$ and $f(y_{k_j}) \to f(x)$, so $d(f(x_{k_j}), f(y_{k_j})) \to 0$. This contradicts the bound $\varepsilon > 0$, so $f$ is uniformly continuous.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $f$ is the local property that compactness makes uniform.
concepts.c:metric-space: Distances on both sides give the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form of uniform continuity.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of the domain turns pointwise continuity into uniform continuity.
concepts.c:uniform-continuity: Uniform continuity is the conclusion: one $\delta$ for each $\varepsilon$.
concepts.c:subsequence: A convergent subsequence locates the point where continuity fails.
concepts.c:seq-compact-space: Sequential compactness of the domain supplies the convergent subsequence.

source.note: The classical proof by contradiction with sequential compactness (Bolzano–Weierstrass), as found in most real analysis textbooks.

statement: Let $X$ be a real [random variable](c:random-variable) with $a \le X \le b$ almost surely and $\mathbb{E} X = 0$. Then its [moment generating function](c:moment-generating-function) satisfies $\mathbb{E}\, e^{tX} \le \exp\big(t^2 (b - a)^2/8\big)$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

hypotheses.text: The variable satisfies $a \le X \le b$ [almost surely](c:almost-everywhere).
The [expected value](c:expected-value) of $X$ is $0$.

conclusion: The variable $X$ is [sub-Gaussian](c:has-subgaussian-mgf) with variance proxy $(b - a)^2/4$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the bound as the sub-Gaussian property with parameter $((b - a)/2)^2$, which also records that $e^{tX}$ is integrable; the bound is the same.

proofs.name: Cumulant function and tilted variance
proofs.slogan: Expand the cumulant generating function to second order and bound its second derivative, a variance under a tilted law, by $((b - a)/2)^2$.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma. The main steps treat $t > 0$, and a sign change of $X$ handles $t < 0$.

roles.why: Boundedness makes $K$ finite and smooth and keeps $X$ in $[a, b]$ under the tilted law.
Zero mean gives $K'(0) = 0$, and it passes to $-X$ in the sign change.

steps.slogan: Define the [cumulant](c:cumulant) generating function $K(s) = \log \mathbb{E}\, e^{sX}$ and record $K(0) = K'(0) = 0$.
steps.detail: Boundedness of $X$ makes $\mathbb{E}\, e^{sX}$ finite and smooth in $s$. Then $K(0) = \log 1 = 0$ and $K'(0) = \mathbb{E} X = 0$.

steps.slogan: Apply Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder to $K$ on $[0, t]$.
Identify $K''(u)$ as the [variance](c:variance) of $X$ under the tilted law $e^{uX}\,d\mathbb{P}/\mathbb{E}\, e^{uX}$.
steps.detail: Differentiating twice gives $K''(u) = \mathbb{E}_u[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}_u X)^2$, where $\mathbb{E}_u$ is the expectation under the tilted law. The tilted law is a probability measure absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathbb{P}$, so $X \in [a, b]$ almost surely under it too.

steps.slogan: Bound the variance of a variable with values in $[a, b]$ by $((b - a)/2)^2$.
steps.detail: For any probability law, $\mathrm{Var}\,X \le \mathbb{E}\big(X - \tfrac{a + b}{2}\big)^2 \le \big(\tfrac{b - a}{2}\big)^2$, because the mean minimizes the mean square deviation and $|X - \tfrac{a + b}{2}| \le \tfrac{b - a}{2}$.

steps.slogan: Reduce negative $t$ to positive $t$ by replacing $X$ with $-X$.
steps.detail: The variable $-X$ has mean $0$ and lies in $[-b, -a]$, an interval of the same length, and $\mathbb{E}\, e^{tX} = \mathbb{E}\, e^{(-t)(-X)}$. The case $t = 0$ is the equality $1 = 1$.

steps.slogan: Exponentiate the bound $K(t) \le (b - a)^2 t^2/8$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 to 4 give $K(t) \le \tfrac{(b - a)^2}{4} \cdot \tfrac{t^2}{2}$ for $t > 0$, and step 5 extends this to every real $t$. So $\mathbb{E}\, e^{tX} = e^{K(t)} \le e^{t^2 (b - a)^2/8}$.

proofs.name: Chord bound and a one-variable estimate
proofs.slogan: Bound $e^{tx}$ by its chord on $[a, b]$, take expectations, and bound the resulting function of one variable by Taylor's theorem.
proofs.scope: The case $a < b$, where zero mean forces $a \le 0 \le b$. If $a = b$, then $X = 0$ almost surely and both sides equal $1$.

roles.why: Boundedness puts $X$ in the interval where the chord bound holds.
Zero mean removes the linear term and fixes the weights of the chord bound.

steps.slogan: Bound the [convex function](c:convex-function) $x \mapsto e^{tx}$ on $[a, b]$ by its chord.
steps.detail: For $x \in [a, b]$, convexity gives $e^{tx} \le \tfrac{b - x}{b - a}\, e^{ta} + \tfrac{x - a}{b - a}\, e^{tb}$, and this holds for $x = X$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: Take expectations and write the bound as $e^{L(h)}$ with $h = t(b - a)$.
steps.detail: With $\mathbb{E} X = 0$ and $\theta = -a/(b - a) \in [0, 1]$, the bound becomes $\mathbb{E}\, e^{tX} \le (1 - \theta)e^{ta} + \theta e^{tb} = e^{L(h)}$, where $L(h) = -\theta h + \log(1 - \theta + \theta e^h)$.

steps.slogan: Compute $L(0) = L'(0) = 0$ and bound $L''$ by $1/4$.
steps.detail: Direct differentiation gives $L'(h) = -\theta + s$ and $L''(h) = s(1 - s)$ with $s = \theta e^h/(1 - \theta + \theta e^h) \in [0, 1]$. So $L(0) = L'(0) = 0$ and $L''(h) \le 1/4$.

steps.slogan: Apply Taylor's theorem to get $L(h) \le h^2/8$ and conclude.
steps.detail: Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder gives $L(h) = L''(\xi)\,h^2/2 \le h^2/8 = t^2 (b - a)^2/8$. With step 2 this gives $\mathbb{E}\, e^{tX} \le e^{t^2 (b - a)^2/8}$.

statement: Let $\varphi\colon G \to H$ be a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism), $S$ a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $G$, and $N \le K$ [normal subgroups](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$. Then $G/\ker\varphi \cong \varphi(G)$, $SN/N \cong S/(S \cap N)$ and $(G/N)/(K/N) \cong G/K$, by isomorphisms induced by $\varphi$ and by the quotient maps.

hypotheses.text: The map $\varphi\colon G \to H$ is a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism).
The set $S$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $G$.
The subgroups $N$ and $K$ are [normal](c:normal-subgroup) in $G$, with $N \le K$.

conclusion: The [quotient groups](c:quotient-group) satisfy the first, second and third isomorphism theorems.

formal.difference: The declaration gives the first isomorphism theorem only. The second and third are the separate declarations QuotientGroup.quotientInfEquivProdNormalQuotient and QuotientGroup.quotientQuotientEquivQuotient.

proofs.name: First theorem, then surjections
proofs.slogan: Prove the first theorem with the map induced on cosets, then apply it to two surjective homomorphisms to get the second and third.
proofs.scope: Groups. The same steps work for rings, modules and other algebraic structures with kernels.

roles.why: The homomorphism property makes the kernel normal and the induced map a homomorphism.
The subgroup $S$ is the domain of the map in the second theorem.
Normality makes $G/N$ and $G/K$ groups, and $N \le K$ makes $gN \mapsto gK$ well defined.

steps.slogan: Show that the [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) of $\varphi$ is a normal subgroup.
steps.detail: For $k \in \ker\varphi$ and $g \in G$, $\varphi(g k g^{-1}) = \varphi(g)\varphi(k)\varphi(g)^{-1} = e$. So $\ker\varphi$ is normal and $G/\ker\varphi$ is a group.

steps.slogan: Define $\bar\varphi(g \ker\varphi) = \varphi(g)$ and check that it is an isomorphism onto the [image](c:image).
steps.detail: One has $\varphi(g) = \varphi(h)$ exactly when $h^{-1} g \in \ker\varphi$, so $\bar\varphi$ is well defined and injective. It is a homomorphism because $\varphi$ is one, and its image is $\varphi(G)$.

steps.slogan: Apply the first theorem to the map $S \to SN/N$, $s \mapsto sN$.
steps.detail: As $N$ is normal, $SN$ is a subgroup that contains $N$, and $snN = sN$ makes the map onto $SN/N$. Its kernel is $S \cap N$, so $S/(S \cap N) \cong SN/N$.

steps.slogan: Apply the first theorem to the map $G/N \to G/K$, $gN \mapsto gK$.
steps.detail: The map is well defined because $N \le K$, and it is a surjective homomorphism. Its kernel is $K/N$, which is therefore normal, so $(G/N)/(K/N) \cong G/K$.

steps.slogan: Collect the three isomorphisms into the statement.
steps.detail: Steps 2, 3 and 4 give the first, second and third isomorphism theorems. Each isomorphism is induced by $\varphi$ or by a quotient map.

concepts.c:group-homomorphism: The first theorem describes what a homomorphism does to $G$.
concepts.c:subgroup: The second theorem compares a subgroup with a normal subgroup.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normal subgroups are exactly the ones with quotient groups.
concepts.c:quotient-group: All three theorems identify quotient groups up to isomorphism.
concepts.c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism: The kernel is the normal subgroup that the first theorem divides out.
concepts.c:image: The image is the group that $G/\ker\varphi$ is isomorphic to.
